passage:
Social science teacher's note, Class 10:
Ahead of the local elections, I asked students to bring one political claim they'd seen online. Pema brought a forwarded image claiming a candidate had built "100 new schools." Abhinav said it was obviously true because many people had shared it. I asked them to check: where did the number come from? Pema found the district education website listed twelve new schools in five years. Abhinav was quiet, then said, "So someone just made it up?" Pema said maybe they counted repairs. We discussed how elected councils decide on schools and how citizens can ask for records.
Next step: the class will write questions for a candidates' public meeting. Pema has volunteered to lead.

qa.q: How many new schools did the district education website list?
qa.a: It listed twelve new schools in five years.

qa.q: What does Abhinav's quiet moment suggest?
qa.a: It suggests Abhinav was surprised and a bit unsettled to find that something widely shared wasn't accurate.

qa.q: What did the teacher's approach teach well?
qa.a: Asking students to trace where a number came from and connecting it to how councils work taught them to check claims instead of trusting shares.

qa.q: How might a candidate see students' questions at the public meeting?
qa.a: They might be impressed, or uncomfortable, since informed questions based on real records are harder to answer with slogans.

grounding: A teacher's note shows teens checking a political claim against public records and learning how local governance works.

passage:
Wednesday
Today in civics class we did a mock election. Afreen and I were in different "parties" and had to make posters. Mine said our party would give free laptops to everyone. The teacher asked, "How will you pay for it?" I had no idea 😅
Afreen's party promised better bus routes, and she had actually worked out which roads need them. She won.
At home, Papa was watching the news and a leader said something big about jobs. I asked, "How will they pay for it?" Papa laughed and said, "Good question." I still don't get how budgets work, but I'm going to ask Afreen. She seems to know.
Pema

qa.q: What did Pema's party promise?
qa.a: Pema's party promised free laptops to everyone.

qa.q: How did Pema feel when the teacher asked how Pema would pay for it?
qa.a: Pema felt caught off guard and a bit embarrassed, with no idea at all.

qa.q: How is Pema starting to read news more critically?
qa.a: Pema is asking how big promises will be paid for, the same question that exposed the weakness in Pema's own poster.

qa.q: How might Afreen see the mock election?
qa.a: She probably enjoyed it and felt her careful planning paid off, and may be happy to explain budgets to Pema.

grounding: A teen's diary shows Pema learning through a mock election to question political promises.

passage: Two weeks before the panchayat election in their village near Nashik, a video began circulating: a candidate standing beside a new school building, captioned 'He built this!' Jeevan, seventeen, watched it three times at the tea stall. Something bothered him. The school looked exactly like the one in the next district. His sister Rashmi, nineteen and voting for the first time, asked, 'So should I vote for him?' 'Let's check first,' Jeevan said. They went to the gram panchayat office and asked to see the list of works done. The school wasn't on it. 'So the video is false?' 'This part is. Doesn't mean he's bad. Just check his real work, and the others' too.' Rashmi nodded and borrowed the list.

qa.q: Where did Jeevan and Rashmi go to check the claim?
qa.a: The gram panchayat office, where they asked for the list of works done.

qa.q: What made Jeevan suspicious of the video?
qa.a: He noticed the school looked like one in the next district, so something felt off.

qa.q: What did Jeevan do well as Rashmi prepared to vote?
qa.a: He checked the claim at the source and kept his conclusion fair, not deciding for her.

qa.q: How might Rashmi approach future campaign videos after this?
qa.a: She might check official records before believing them, as a first-time voter learning how local government works.

grounding: Shows a rural teen checking a political claim and learning how local elections and records work.

passage: In Johannesburg, Lindiwe, seventeen, was reading two news sites about the city council's vote to raise water tariffs. One headline said, 'Council Robs Residents!' The other said, 'Council Approves Tariff Change After Drought Warnings.' She frowned and messaged Sami from civics class: 'Same story, totally different vibe.' Sami replied, 'Check the actual council minutes. They're public.' That evening she found them online. Forty councillors had voted; the reasons were listed, and some had objected. She also found out her ward councillor's name for the first time. Lindiwe turns eighteen next year. She added a reminder on her phone: 'Register to vote.' Then she emailed her councillor a question about the drought plan.

qa.q: What were the two headlines Lindiwe read about the council?
qa.a: 'Council Robs Residents!' and 'Council Approves Tariff Change After Drought Warnings.'

qa.q: How did Lindiwe feel reading the two different headlines?
qa.a: She was puzzled and a bit suspicious, noticing the same story was told with very different emotion.

qa.q: Which of Lindiwe's steps could any young reader copy?
qa.a: Comparing sources, reading the original public record and contacting their representative with a question.

qa.q: How might Lindiwe's councillor see an email from a young resident?
qa.a: The councillor might be pleased, or at least reminded that young future voters are paying attention.

grounding: Shows a teen outside India reading news critically and learning how local governance and voting work.

At the school civics club, Zubin, sixteen, held up his phone. “Look, a forwarded message says the candidate from Ward 12 promised free laptops for every student.”
Tejas, the club secretary, frowned. “Where's it from?”
“My uncle's group.”
They checked. The candidate's own printed pamphlet, which Tejas had collected, said nothing about laptops. The local newspaper's interview didn't either. The message had no source, no date.
Zubin felt his face go hot. He'd already forwarded it to three friends.
He messaged them: That laptop thing is not confirmed. Sorry.
In the mock election that afternoon, the club made a rule: every claim on the board needs a source.

qa.q: What did the forwarded message claim?
qa.a: That the candidate from Ward 12 promised free laptops for every student.

qa.q: How did Zubin feel when he realised the message was false?
qa.a: He felt embarrassed, his face going hot, because he had already forwarded it.

qa.q: What did Zubin and Tejas do to check the claim?
qa.a: They compared it with the candidate's printed pamphlet and the newspaper interview, and noticed it had no source.

qa.q: How might Zubin's friends feel getting his correction?
qa.a: They may appreciate his honesty and be more careful about forwards too.

grounding: A sixteen-year-old learns to check a political claim before sharing and helps set a source rule.

passage:
Dear Hansa,
You asked me how voting works because you're doing a project. I voted for the first time last month, so here's what I learned.
Before the day, I checked my name on the voter list online. At the booth in our school, an officer checked my ID, put ink on my finger, and I pressed a button on the machine next to the candidate I chose. A little slip showed my choice for a few seconds, then dropped into a box. Nobody could see who I voted for.
The week before, a video went round claiming one candidate had been arrested. I checked two newspapers. Neither reported it. It was fake.
My advice: read more than one source, and look at what candidates actually promise.
Your cousin, Gargi

qa.q: Where was the polling booth?
qa.a: In their school.

qa.q: How did Gargi seem to feel about voting for the first time?
qa.a: Gargi seemed proud and interested, eager to explain it.

qa.q: What advice does Gargi give Hansa about political claims?
qa.a: Read more than one source and look at what candidates actually promise.

qa.q: How might Hansa feel reading this letter?
qa.a: Hansa may feel excited and better prepared for the project and for voting one day.

grounding: A young voter explains to a younger cousin how voting works and how to check a false claim.

passage:
Vandana, you asked how I got interested in politics. It wasn't the TV debates. They just made me angry.
At seventeen, our municipal councillor held an open meeting about the broken drains in our ward. My mother dragged me along. I'm Gautam, and I expected shouting.
Instead, I saw how things actually work. The councillor explained which money comes from the state and which from the city. An engineer showed the plan. Residents asked hard questions. The councillor promised a date, and wrote it on a board.
Three months later, the drains were done. I went back to the next meeting on my own.
Now I read two newspapers that disagree with each other every morning. I don't trust any single one.

qa.q: What was the open meeting about?
qa.a: The broken drains in their ward.

qa.q: How did Gautam feel about TV debates?
qa.a: Gautam felt angry and put off by them.

qa.q: What did Gautam learn from the meeting, and how does it shape Gautam's news habits?
qa.a: How local government actually works, which led Gautam to read two newspapers that disagree, instead of trusting one.

qa.q: How might the councillor feel seeing Gautam return to the next meeting?
qa.a: The councillor may feel encouraged that a young person is taking an interest.

grounding: A seventeen-year-old learns how local governance works and starts reading news critically.

I'm Harish, and I sat next to Rajni in the Class 11 common room when a video went round the group: "Breaking: Voting date changed, go vote tomorrow instead!"
Rajni's grandmother was going to vote. Rajni frowned and didn't forward it. She opened the Election Commission website on her phone, scrolled, and said, "The date is the same. This is fake."
Then she typed in the group: "Checked the official site. Date hasn't changed. Please don't forward."
A few people reacted with thumbs up. One person said she was being preachy.
I don't know if she was angry or just worried about her Nani. But she stayed calm and posted the link.

qa.q: Which website did Rajni check?
qa.a: The Election Commission website.

qa.q: What might Rajni have been feeling when she frowned at the video?
qa.a: Rajni was probably worried and suspicious, thinking of her grandmother who planned to vote.

qa.q: What did Rajni do that others could learn from?
qa.a: She didn't forward the video, checked the official source, and shared the correct link calmly.

qa.q: How does Harish see Rajni's reaction?
qa.a: Harish can't tell exactly how Rajni feels but sees her stay calm and use facts.

grounding: A classmate watches a teen check a false voting claim against the official source.

Varun, you're asking why I get so serious about voting. Let me tell you about my first time.
I was nineteen. Someone in the market said, "If you vote for the wrong party, your ration card will be cancelled." Everyone believed it. I was scared.
I went to our teacher, Master-ji. He said, "Your vote is secret. Nobody can know. And no party can cancel your card for how you voted." He showed me the rules in a book.
So I voted. For the one I thought would fix our road. That party lost. But the road got fixed anyway, two years later.
Your Bhupen dada learned: check the rumour, then vote without fear.

qa.q: What did someone in the market say would happen if you voted for the wrong party?
qa.a: Your ration card will be cancelled.

qa.q: What was young Bhupen feeling after hearing the rumour?
qa.a: Bhupen felt scared that his vote could cost the family the ration card.

qa.q: What choice inside the story helped young Bhupen vote without fear?
qa.a: He chose to check the rumour with Master-ji, who showed him the rules about the secret ballot.

qa.q: How might Master-ji have felt helping young Bhupen?
qa.a: Master-ji probably felt glad to clear up the rumour and help a young person vote.

grounding: A grandfather tells how he checked a voting rumour before his first vote.

passage:
Two days before the municipal election, Neelam's grandfather, Ramesh, got a message on the family group: "The new flyover was built only by Party A. Party B blocked it for years!" He was about to forward it to his 200-member community group.
"Wait, Dadu," Neelam said. "Where's it from?"
"Everyone is sharing it."
The power had gone and her phone was at 8%. She had to be quick. She searched the city corporation's website for the project page. It said the flyover was approved by the full council, with both parties voting for it, and delayed by land disputes.
She showed him before the phone died.
Dadu frowned. "So it's half true, half nonsense."
"More nonsense, I think."
He didn't forward it. Instead, he typed in the family group: "Check before sending, it's election time."

qa.q: What did the city corporation's website say about the flyover?
qa.a: It said it was approved by the full council with both parties voting for it, and delayed by land disputes.

qa.q: What does Dadu's frown at the website suggest?
qa.a: It suggests Dadu felt surprised and uneasy, realising he'd nearly spread a misleading claim.

qa.q: What was the key step Neelam took, and why?
qa.a: Checking an official source before sharing, because popularity doesn't make a claim true, especially near an election.

qa.q: How might the 200-member group have been affected if Dadu had forwarded it?
qa.a: Many people could have believed a false story about the parties just before voting.

grounding: Illustrates a teen checking a political claim against an official source under time pressure.

passage:
On election morning in their Hyderabad colony, Rajni, voting for the first time, dragged her sister Alka along to the polling booth at the school.
Alka had only seen elections on the news, all shouting. Here it was a queue under a tree, an old man with a newspaper, a volunteer helping an elderly woman.
Inside, Alka watched through the door as an official checked Rajni's voter card and name on a list. Another put ink on her finger. Then Rajni went behind a screen, alone.
"Why alone?" Alka whispered to the volunteer.
"So nobody can see or pressure you. Your vote is secret."
Afterward Rajni held up her inked finger, grinning. "Nobody knows who I voted for. Not even you."
Alka looked at the queue again. "Can I come with you next time too?"

qa.q: What did the official put on Rajni's finger?
qa.a: The official put ink on her finger.

qa.q: How did Alka feel by the end of the morning?
qa.a: Alka felt curious and interested, and wanted to come along next time.

qa.q: How could a parent or teacher build on Alka's experience?
qa.a: They could explain why the vote is secret and how votes are counted, using what she saw at the booth.

qa.q: How might Rajni feel voting for the first time?
qa.a: Rajni seems proud and excited, grinning with her inked finger and happy her choice is her own.

grounding: Shows a teen observing how voting works and learning why a secret ballot matters.

passage:
"Look at this." Raghav held out his phone. "'City water crisis: taps run dry across the city.'"
Jaya scrolled on hers. "Mine says, 'Water supply cut in three wards for pipeline repair.'"
"Same day?"
"Same day. Same story, I think."
"'Across the city' sounds a lot worse."
"And gets more clicks." Jaya tapped. "Which ones have the ward numbers? The official notice?"
"Mine doesn't."
"Mine links the water board's notice. Three wards. Two days."
Raghav frowned. "So the first one isn't lying exactly. It's just… bigger."
"It makes people panic. And there's an election next month. Blaming someone works better if everything sounds worse."
"So we check the source, not just the headline."
"And who's saying it, and why."

qa.q: How many wards did the second headline say were affected?
qa.a: Three wards.

qa.q: What does Raghav's frown suggest about how he felt?
qa.a: Raghav felt uneasy and a bit misled, noticing that the first headline had made the problem sound bigger.

qa.q: What could Raghav and Jaya do before sharing a news story next time?
qa.a: Look for the official notice or source, compare headlines, and ask who benefits from the way it's framed.

qa.q: How might people who only read the first headline react?
qa.a: They might panic about the whole city's water or blame someone before knowing it was a short, local repair.

grounding: Illustrates teens comparing headlines about the same event and reading news critically, especially near an election.

passage:
A week before the municipal elections last year, a message landed in our family group: a photo of a candidate with the words "He will close all government schools!" My uncle forwarded it to everyone. I'm Wasim, and I was sixteen and didn't know how to check anything.
My friend Arnab said, "Where's the source? A photo with words isn't news."
So we looked. We found the candidate's actual speech on a local news site. He'd said he wanted to merge two small schools, not close all of them. Big difference.
I showed my uncle. He grumbled, but he deleted the forward.
That made me curious, so I read how the ward councillor is chosen and what they actually control. Roads, water, drains, not national laws.
Next year, I can vote for the first time. I want to know what I'm voting for.

qa.q: What did the candidate actually say in his speech?
qa.a: He'd said he wanted to merge two small schools, not close all of them.

qa.q: What was Wasim's uncle feeling when shown the real speech?
qa.a: The uncle felt a bit annoyed and embarrassed, grumbling, but accepted the truth enough to delete the forward.

qa.q: How could someone check a political claim like this?
qa.a: Ask where the source is, find the original speech or a reliable news report, and compare the claim with what was actually said.

qa.q: Why might Arnab react differently to the forward than Wasim's uncle?
qa.a: Arnab questioned it right away because a photo with words isn't news, while the uncle trusted it and passed it on.

grounding: Shows a teenager checking a political claim against the source and learning how local government and voting work.
